title: Firmwide AI training and certification, with tool access gated on completion
problem: New lawyers form AI habits before firm guidance reaches them, and 34% of surveyed professionals use AI tools their organisation has not sanctioned.
approach: Training and a written policy become a condition of access to AI tools, repeated as tools change.
PwC says over 330,000 people have taken AI training and Accenture over 550,000 (self-reported); Deloitte and Anthropic announced certification for 15,000.
Training must be completed before access is granted, and refreshed when tools or their autonomy change.
who: PwC, Accenture, Deloitte, Latham & Watkins, Blank Rome

title: Onboarding rebuilt for new associates, with AI champions and a first-draft rule
problem: AI is absorbing the routine tasks that built associates' judgment, so a one-time training session no longer develops either AI practice or judgment.
approach: Duane Morris runs a two-day orientation then twice-monthly sessions; each practice group has AI champions who show new lawyers suitable tools.
One fixed principle: a first draft is never an appropriate final submission. No outcome measures are published.
A separate mentorship track remains, and the talent team debriefs each outgoing class to redesign the next programme.

title: Protected billable-credit time and build competitions for junior lawyers to learn AI
problem: Training time competes with billable targets, so juniors have little protected time to learn AI tools while AI takes over their routine tasks.
approach: Ropes & Gray lets first-year associates spend up to 20% of billable hours (reported as nearly 400 a year) learning AI tools.
Extended to Europe in January 2026; an AI World Cup drew 25 teams building workflows for real problems (self-reported).
Partners hear junior presentations and lead mentoring circles; progress is reported regularly.

title: Rotations and secondments putting juniors inside AI, innovation and knowledge teams
problem: Juniors need a development path when drafting and diligence no longer fill the day, and firms need people who understand both the practice and the AI tools.
approach: A&O Shearman associates work inside its Markets Innovation Group; from September 2026 Sidley London trainees do a seat in its AI lab.
MinterEllison's accelerator produced more than 150 use cases, and over a thousand employees logged in on day one (vendor-published).
Outputs are checked against the playbook, and trainees work alongside practice lawyers and knowledge, research and data staff.
who: A&O Shearman, Sidley, MinterEllison, Stephenson Harwood

title: AI training moved upstream: funded master's degrees, vendor academies, law-school programmes
problem: New lawyers often arrive with little AI experience, so training falls on employers and delays use on client work.
approach: Freshfields funds a King's College London LL.M in Law & Technology for future trainees, with a GBP 20,000 maintenance grant.
Harvey launched Harvey Academy in January 2026 and says it works with 100+ law schools; Legora has nine founding schools (vendor-published).
Freshfields keeps a continued firm connection with trainees during their studies.

title: AI practice environments replacing lost junior repetitions: simulations, personas, pre-review feedback
problem: When AI does routine drafting or review, juniors lose the repetitions and feedback loops that built judgment, and seniors have little time to coach.
approach: Kennedys and Spellbook are launching simulated learning scenarios; Three Crowns worked with Stanford on a cross-examination simulator.
Duane Morris uses a ChatGPT-based tool to rehearse hard feedback; a BYU professor built an Excel review tool. No measures published.
Mentors coach using simulation feedback, and managers still review after the junior's self-check.
who: Kennedys, Duane Morris, Three Crowns, Ascend, BYU

title: Entry-level roles redesigned so juniors review and supervise AI output earlier
problem: Entry-level work such as data gathering is being taken over by AI, removing the work that taught execution first and judgment later.
approach: PwC's AI assurance leader said new hires will oversee AI on routine audit tasks and become reviewers quickly; Withum pushes responsibilities down.
PwC job-ad analysis finds AI-exposed junior roles 7 times more likely to ask for senior skills (vendor-published).
Reviewers sign off AI-performed tasks, and managers question trainees on their reasoning even when the result is right.

title: Graduate and associate programmes rebuilt around earlier judgment and human skills
problem: Graduates' first-year work of data entry and basic reports is being automated, so the old sequence of manual tasks first and judgment later no longer fits.
approach: City AM reports all UK Big Four firms overhauled graduate training; KPMG front-loads exams so graduates advise clients in year two.
Winston Taylor taught 12 durable skills partly with a theatre company; Sheppard hired an AI-mindset trainer. No outcome measures published.
Graduates learn alongside experienced staff and partners before client engagements.
who: KPMG, PwC, Winston Taylor, Sheppard, Duane Morris

title: Teaching and checking verification and independent reasoning explicitly
problem: Most AI training teaches what tools do, not when to trust, verify or override them, yet professionals are held accountable for AI-assisted work.
approach: Fredrikson & Byron states a goal of a formal curriculum on supervising AI output; PKF Smith Cooper managers question trainees' correct results.
Proposals include aviation-style verification checklists, assigned challengers and AI-off days. In one survey, 72% cited gaps in deep legal reasoning (vendor-published).
A reviewer questions the junior's reasoning, and someone other than the drafter challenges it.
who: Fredrikson & Byron, PKF Smith Cooper, Barbri

title: Junior AI-use disclosure and second-level supervisor review
problem: Juniors can submit polished AI-assisted work without checking sources or telling the supervisor; in one UK case, fictitious authorities reached the court.
approach: Juniors tell supervisors when AI was used, verify every authority and quote, and escalate errors at once, per DWF's published guide.
The solicitors' regulator received 42 reports of AI misuse in the past year (independent).
Supervisors carry out second-level review with sources checked, and a lawyer approves any filing.
who: DWF, UK regulator and bar bodies

title: Measuring whether juniors keep building expertise under AI, using a no-AI test
problem: AI can raise the quality of delivered work while stunting the expertise professionals would develop by doing it, and firms have lacked controlled measurement.
approach: A three-month randomised trial gave 133 patent lawyers at eleven US IP firms a custom AI drafting assistant; experts scored work blind.
Quality rose +0.34 SD at 10 days, +0.38 SD at 90 days (vendor-published); on a no-AI task, juniors showed no average gain.
The design can serve as a template for a firm-level check on skill formation.

title: Skill-aware task allocation: use AI where juniors gain, teach where it fails
problem: Gains from AI differ by task and baseline skill, and outside AI's competence it can make results worse, so firms need evidence on which tasks to protect.
approach: Controlled-experiment evidence sets task rules and teaches the boundary of reliable use; 758 BCG consultants were tested in a preregistered experiment.
Inside the frontier: 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster; outside it: 19% less likely to be correct (independent).
Human review of any task flagged as outside the AI frontier.
who: BCG, Harvard Business School, University of Minnesota

title: Recruiting and assessing for judgment and learning agility, not credentials
problem: AI makes surface competence easy to show, so hiring proxies such as grades and tool knowledge say less about who will perform when the answer is unclear.
approach: Fredrikson & Byron prioritises curiosity over tool checklists; McKinsey is reported to use an AI interview where finalists prompt Lilli.
The McKinsey report comes from a preparation firm and the Financial Times; McKinsey declined to comment. No outcome measures published.
Interviewers judge how a candidate reasons, not whether the answer is right.

title: AI-led screening interviews for graduate applicants, under bias-audit and human-review rules
problem: Application forms limit what candidates can say, and recruiters make early screening decisions from thin information.
approach: Mishcon de Reya is trialling Bright Apply for its 2026 graduate season: a tailored, untimed virtual interview replacing a long form.
Almost 75% of students rated it 4 or 5 out of 5 (self-reported).
The firm reviews each transcript and its Early Careers team makes all screening decisions; regulators expect bias audits and notice.

title: AI adoption written into objectives, performance reviews and promotion
problem: Firms that have invested in AI cannot capture value unless staff use it, and only 39% of professionals have personal goals linked to AI adoption.
approach: KPMG tracks AI use through tool data and will assess staff on AI objectives in 2026 performance reviews.
Accenture reportedly collects senior staff's weekly AI log-ins and requires regular adoption for leadership; PwC's US CEO said resisters have no place.
Managers set and review year-end objectives; how usage is weighed in promotion was not published.

title: Firmwide bonus pool tied to staff AI prompt volume
problem: A general-purpose AI tool delivers little unless many people use it, and the firm wanted to encourage everyday use without mandating it.
approach: Shoosmiths set a target of one million Microsoft Copilot prompts within its firmwide bonus scheme, unlocking an extra GBP 1 million.
The firm reached 1,000,000 prompts more than four months early (self-reported).
Payout was conditional on the firm meeting its core financial metric.

title: AI in associate reviews; scoring for pay or promotion is an idea
problem: Associate evaluations take a great deal of time and feedback often arrives stale; AI scoring of people brings the same legal duties as hiring.
approach: Of 106 US and Canadian firms surveyed, 31% had integrated AI into evaluations, mostly for summaries, feedback analysis and bias checks (independent).
Using AI indicators for promotion, training selection or pay was not found deployed in professional services.
Supervising lawyers write the comments, and a human reviews every adverse outcome.

title: Professional-grade AI access as a recruiting and retention lever
problem: Professionals who see a gap between AI's value to the organisation and to themselves are more likely to consider leaving.
approach: Provide approved professional-grade tools, communicate the AI strategy, and tie AI value to recognition and progression.
24% considering leaving within two years; USD 232,000 per replacement (Thomson Reuters estimate, vendor-published).
Recruiters are prepared to explain tools, workflow fit and career impact.

title: Resizing entry-level intake as AI absorbs junior work
problem: The leverage pyramid rested on large junior cohorts doing work that both billed and trained; if AI absorbs it, firms must decide how many entrants to hire.
approach: Three positions: smaller intake, more laterals, or held intake with a redesigned role. UK Big Four hiring fell; KPMG 1,399 to 942.
Two-thirds of 57 large US firms surveyed by Citi expect fewer first-years in 2028 than in 2025 (independent).
A partner, board or talent committee decides class size, reviewed annually against demand and client pressure.
who: Big Four, McKinsey, large US law firms

title: Leverage and workforce model redesigned for hybrid human-and-agent teams
problem: AI compresses the junior layer and clients are reluctant to pay for junior tasks, while resource managers lack playbooks for teams mixing experts and agents.
approach: A quarter of law firms expect leverage changes by 2027; McKinsey's chief executive has said it has 20,000 agents alongside 40,000 staff.
In one survey, 74% of law firms plan flat headcount using AI and 14% expect agents to do most work (vendor-published).
Partners and management committees decide structure, and resource managers approve team composition.

title: Upskilling plus compressed-timeline exits where reskilling is not viable
problem: For some staff, reskilling is not a viable path to the skills the firm needs, and strategy, structure and performance measures were not aligned.
approach: Accenture announced a six-month optimisation programme with up to USD 865 million of related charges and a talent strategy: upskill, exit, efficiency.
Expected savings above USD 1 billion (self-reported); headcount is still expected to rise overall.
No human checkpoints are stated in the sources.

title: Support-function roles re-scoped as AI and hub operations take routine work
problem: Finance, HR, IT, marketing and secretarial support teams carry routine work that AI and hub operations can take over.
approach: Clifford Chance told London business-services staff greater use of AI meant jobs had to go; about 10% of 550 affected (independent).
Baker McKenzie says a review of its business professionals functions means some roles will likely be phased out and others will evolve.
Consultation processes apply in relevant jurisdictions before changes are final.

title: Idea: new junior operational roles as an apprenticeship route
problem: Idea, not a deployment: if drafting and research are cheap, junior work moves to operations, data and verification, and firms need a defined route into it.
approach: A Thomson Reuters Institute columnist proposes rotating junior lawyers through AI compliance, legal data analysis, knowledge curation and workflow-prototyping roles.
A related suggestion is rotations through knowledge management, professional development and technology functions.
Progression to strategic roles would be supervised.

title: Idea: milestone-based progression, deliberate-mistake exercises and measures beyond billable hours
problem: Idea, not a deployment: time-served progression assumed judgment would emerge from repetition, so firms need another way to develop and certify readiness.
approach: A consultant proposes milestones, with early-career staff learning through returns with buried issues, plausible-but-wrong AI recommendations and client-meeting debriefs.
A LexisNexis survey found leaders rank revenue growth (55%) and client feedback (49%) above billable hours (38%) (vendor-published).
Debriefs ask what the person noticed and missed; partners and talent committees approve new metrics.

title: Idea: residency-style supervised practice and a funded profession-wide formation system
problem: Idea, not a deployment: AI reduces traditional first jobs, and the profession has no agreed definition of legal judgment or standards for AI use in training.
approach: A Thomson Reuters Institute white paper proposes work-based learning modelled on medical residencies, teaching judgment as micro-skills with AI as thinking partner.
Funding might come from a small percentage of legal services revenue; Northeastern Law and UNH Franklin Pierce are cited as existing models.
Supervised postgraduate practice would form part of licensure (proposed).
